extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public administration; Forest Service and other government managers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing and operating an administrative control system, illustrated by the U.S. Forest Service's practices (delegation, classification of correspondence, inspections, manuals, budgets, and operating studies). Intended to inform managers on how to apply control without overcentralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Span of control principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid creating too large a work load for the executive by going into excessive detail or insisting on case-by-case clearance rather than relying on inspection, reports, and conferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Span of control is determined more by the volume of control work than by number of people. An official closely supervising three subordinates (signing all their mail, reviewing each act) may have more to do than one giving policy supervision to eight or ten. Managers should avoid excessive case-by-case clearance and use inspection and reporting mechanisms instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planned delegation
rubrics_metrics.description: As much as possible should be handled as far down the line as possible, while administrators and division chiefs retain personal supervision over matters involving over-all or divisional policy or which transcend subordinates' competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain sufficient delegation without disintegration there must be a well-understood classification of administrative and executive actions (often assignments of signing authority). Delegation must balance decentralization with retention of supervision for policy-level matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working classification of correspondence (general principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a flexible classification of mail that specifies qualitative characteristics of each class and leaves it to subordinates' judgment to determine class membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigid, plurality-of-individual determinations bring insignificant items to high officials' desks. A flexible, principle-based system reduces congestion while applying appropriate control to each communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental correspondence (class 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications to heads of Executive Departments other than Agriculture, to Committees of Congress, and when matters of more than routine import are involved, to heads of Independent Agencies, replies for signature of the Secretary, initial communications involving Departmental policy or matters important enough to warrant signature by the Secretary or Acting Secretary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjected to the highest administrative control: personal review by the Chief of the Service and appropriate officials in the Secretary's Office. Includes determinations of the highest quality, important subject matter, requiring widest technical and administrative competence, and involving grave consequences in case of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service correspondence (class 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications to the Secretary of Agriculture, directors of major departmental divisions, chiefs of other bureaus/agencies when Departmental policy is not involved, Senators/Representatives under certain conditions, and other correspondence warranting signature by the Chief of the Forest Service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receives no departmental clearance but highest control within the bureau; always signed by the Chief or Acting Chief. May be internal (e.g., orders to Regional Foresters establishing bureau policy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional correspondence (class 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications staying within the field of a single division: to Regional Foresters, Directors of Experiment Stations, Forest Products Laboratory, other field units, other divisions of the Chief's Office, or other agencies/individuals on matters not involving policy beyond the division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not subjected to control outside the originating division; divisions in Washington may write directly to regional counterparts on subjects within their field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional forester-director correspondence (class 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters from regional offices and experiment stations dealing with bureau-wide interest in the area, inter-divisional questions, personnel actions, communications to the Chief's Office or other Regional Offices, or matters materially affecting the standing of an appointed employee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signed by the Regional Forester or Director and immediate assistants; more inclusive than service correspondence but less likely to cause congestion due to lower volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field divisional correspondence (class 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: All correspondence with Federal, State, and private agencies dealing with matters within the field of the Division or Office not covered by Departmental, Service, or Regional classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually does not pass through the office of the Regional Forester; divisions write directly to Supervisors of National Forests and outsiders on matters within their field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forest and Ranger District correspondence (classes 6 & 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondence signed in offices of National Forest Supervisors (forest) and District Rangers (ranger district), covering local, routine matters handled at those levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These offices typically do not need formal decentralization; Supervisors may delegate signing of mail in some fields. Control here is minimal and local.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible routing and standard routings for recurrent letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish standard routings for many recurrent letters, but allow the Chief or division chiefs to decide routing for non-routine matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-routine matters, the Chief must decide whether Secretary should sign; division chiefs ensure the Chief receives for review each item important enough to warrant his attention. This supports decentralization while preserving necessary central review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor system of control (conditions for success)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decentralized, honor-based execution works only if certain organizational conditions exist: thorough integrated planning; complete confidence between Chief and assistants; uniformity of purpose, custom, and policy; and clear understanding of jurisdictional boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without these factors, suspicion and friction lead to extended detailed control. The honor system depends on corporate responsibility and voluntary cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a service manual prepared democratically
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a Forest Service Manual that provides service-wide understanding of objectives and operating standards, representing basic experience and objectives of operating units and prepared through a democratic process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divisions prepare original and amendatory text for their fields; Operation edits for arrangement and form; Assistant Chiefs and Chief review and approve text. Questionable policy/features may be previewed by field units before inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional administrative handbooks and technical handbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional Foresters and station Directors should issue administrative handbooks to relate service objectives and standards to local problems; technical handbooks set forth 'best ways' to perform recurrent jobs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field handbooks need not be cleared through Washington but should be integrated with the parent manual to avoid duplication or conflict. Technical handbooks cover fire-fighting, surveying, timber appraisal, range, wildlife, water management, and engineering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning down to district level and project work budgets
rubrics_metrics.description: Planning extends from central office through regional and forest organization to District Rangers; plans are consolidated into 'project work budgets' which incorporate work other than normal year-long personnel activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project and recurrent budgets are based on operating studies and job-load analyses at each level and serve both control and training functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operating studies and job-load analyses (requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operating studies must include: (a) preparation of a carefully drawn-up program covering immediate needs; (b) uniformity of method; (c) rigid regularity in making observations; and (d) adequacy of reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These studies provide data for judging performance and for budgeting, objectifying comparative needs and minimizing fund apportionment based on debating ability. Regions have administrative-studies consultants to review and integrate studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection program: functional and general integrating inspections
rubrics_metrics.description: A comprehensive inspection program: 'functional inspection' by divisional officers for their fields, and 'general integrating inspections' by senior Washington officials to appraise overall progress and translate experience into policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional officials assist inspectors; functional inspectors make recommendations through the Regional Forester to Supervisors to avoid multiple-authority confusion. General inspections occur about once every three years and involve weeks-long visits, consultations with many stakeholders, and cross-cutting evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection assessment framework and focal items
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspectors are instructed to keep in mind fundamental criteria such as: condition of basic resources (soil, living resources), major projects and objectives with past accomplishments and future plans, 'spiritual' qualities of administration (leadership, relationships with users, liaison between research and administration, morale, social philosophy, financial responsibility), organization and financial responsibility, and miscellaneous items (buildings, paper work, public relations, joint activities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors are a framework for arranging and interpreting facts and observations, not an outline for the report. Inspection reports should cover relationships, major resources (forest growth, recreation, wildlife, water, range, land acquisition), landlord roles, organization/financial responsibility, and other operational concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of inspection reports into policy and follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspection reports are considered at staff conferences; the Chief writes a letter transmitting the report to the Regional Forester with general and specific instructions; the Regional Forester responds with comments and steps to comply; the report and Chief's letter become the basis of general policy executed under functional supervision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferably the Chief's letter accompanies the inspection report; inspectors may elaborate as needed during staff consideration. This creates a feedback loop from inspection to policy to execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralized execution requires precise organization and avoidance of overlaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Decentralized execution and control after the fact demand a precisely built organization with no serious overlaps between fields of work and avoidance of conflicting orders through voluntary cooperation between divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because service work consists of closely interlocking functions rather than discrete areas, thoroughgoing voluntary coordination is essential to prevent conflicting authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional lines of authority (authority from function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control should flow along lines of authority that are functional rather than merely hierarchical: each functional officer carries authority and responsibility for his part of an order, and his signature suffices for that part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the subordinate, by possession and presentation of facts, determines the decision, let him make it, subject only to coordinating and precautionary control by the superior executive. Authority should arise from function, i.e., who possesses the facts, not from delegation alone.
